title: Minority Identities in Film and Culture: The Italian American and African American Experience

sections.note: Were Italian Americans white? What is whiteness? How does identity politics define the relation between minority groups? To answer these questions, this course explores films by Italian American and African American directors such as Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, and Spike Lee, as well as short stories and essays by authors such as John Fante and Thomas J. Ferraro. This class will also welcome guest lectures. This course satisfies the General Education Criteria for: Cultural Studies - US Minority

In this course students improve their oral and written competence in Italian using more complex structures and elevated texts than those of Italian 210. They review the principal grammatical structures of Italian, and analyze the connection of form, content, and style. The grammatical structures are always presented in communicative contexts. In the second part of the course students learn about the linguistic repertoire of Italy. They later conduct research on one particular region, and present the research in a mini-presentation for the group. Prerequisite for Ital 310 should be Ital 210 or consent of instructor.

This course examines the evolution of neofascist ideologies, movements, and regimes from 1945 to the present. We will analyze the ideological foundations of neofascism, the role of clandestine networks, and the impact of far-right extremism on contemporary politics. We will also discuss legal, philosophical, and historical debates over neofascist movements. This course involves analysis of primary sources from figures like Julius Evola, Aleksandr Dugin, Francis Parker Yockey, and Savitri Devi, as well as recent scholarship on the topic. (Meets with PS 377) Please note: there are no prerequisites for this class.

Language & Minorities in Europe. Credit: 3 or 4 hours. Survey of regional and immigrant minority language use, policies, and planning across Europe. Focus on political and social issues, such as language regimes, education, loss, and maintenance. Two immigrant languages, Turkish and Arabic/Berber, and four indigenous language families: Balto-Slavic with Estonian, Celtic, Romance with Basque, and Slavic with Hungarian. Taught in English. Same as GER 418, ITAL 418, LING 418, PS 418, SLAV 418, SPAN 418, and EURO 418. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.

Novelist, poet, filmmaker, and polemicist, Pier Paolo Pasolini remains one of the most influential and controversial figures of twentieth-century Italian culture. This course examines the modern Italian novel through a sustained study of Pasolini’s narrative work, from Ragazzi di vita and Una vita violenta to the unfinished Petrolio. Particular attention will be paid to the relationship between his novels and his films: how the Roman borgate, the sacred, dialect, and the body migrate from page to screen, and how Pasolini’s cinema rethinks the problems of realism, language, and narration first posed in his fiction. Readings will be paired with screenings of films such as Accattone, Mamma Roma, and Teorema. This class will also welcome guest lectures.

Topic Title:Discovering Language and Culture in Digital Worlds. This course examines the language and cultures of online spaces, from multiplayer games and livestreaming communities to forums and text-based worlds. Students will explore a community firsthand, share their environments with their fellow students, and develop a research proposal based on what they discover
